scenes.narration: Your morning coffee began as a way to stay awake for midnight prayers. In the 1400s, Sufi monks in Yemen drank it to get through long nights of worship.
Legend says an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi found it after his goats ate red berries and got jumpy. That part is a story, but the coffee plant really does come from Ethiopia.
By the 1500s, coffeehouses had spread across Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul. People went there to talk, play games and argue about politics.
Not everyone liked it. In 1511, the governor of Mecca banned coffee, but the ban did not last.
In the 1600s coffee reached Europe, and London filled with coffeehouses. Lloyd's of London, the famous insurance market, started in one of them.
Europeans then took coffee plants to their colonies. The Dutch grew it on Java, and in 1727 coffee arrived in Brazil.
Today Brazil grows more coffee than any other country. A prayer drink from Yemen now powers the whole world's mornings.
